## Status: reviewed, not yet implemented
Reviewed on 2026-11-12. The review is kept at `reviews/review_02c_eigensolver.md`.
It ran jaxdft itself with an instrumented copy of `lobpcg`, not a separate
NumPy rebuild, because this milestone is about the code's own numerics. It
reproduced every number in the stopping-test and memory tables exactly, and
confirmed the interlacing bound. It changed three things:

- It questioned whether the penalty on dropped directions causes the GPU
  failures, since on the CPU directions are dropped only at the first
  iteration of each call.
- It found a blow-up past the attainable residual. The solver gains a
  stagnation stop and returns its best iterate.
- `EIGEN_FLOOR` is below the attainable residual. It becomes a multiple of
  $\epsilon_\text{mach}\lVert H\rVert$.

It also tightened the adaptive tolerance (non-increasing, per electron, a
latch after refinement), added column chunking to the dense solver, and
answered the open questions. The decisions are recorded at the
[end of this post](#decisions-from-review).

By then three explanations of the GPU failures had been proposed, one each
by the session that ran the cluster diagnosis, the draft of this post and
the review, each on indirect evidence. A per-iteration record of LOBPCG on
the V100 and on two CPUs then decided between them
([evidence](#evidence-per-iteration-on-both-devices)): the penalty is the
cause on the GPU, because the GPU drops directions at every iteration near
convergence. The review's blow-up is real on the CPU once a run goes past
its attainable residual, independently of the penalty, but it is not what
failed on the GPU. The draft's claim that the penalty also causes CPU
stalls was wrong.

The numbers quoted as *scratch checks* come from throwaway copies of
`lobpcg` and of the SCF core on the laptop (commit `3383ca3`). The
validation document repeats them with the implementation.
:::

## Scope

Milestone 2c is a numerical milestone with no new physics. The HPC runs
recorded in the engineering log on 2026-11-12 found three problems. They
block larger k-grids, the GPU, and through both of them every later
milestone (smearing on aluminium, 2D systems):

1. **k-point cost.** The summed eigensolver iterations of an SCF grow with
   the number of k-points, although the k-points are one `vmap` batch. The
   batched eigensolver iterates in lockstep until the slowest k-point has
   converged. On the CPU this makes the time per k-point and SCF step grow
   5.6 times from 1 to 512 k-points. On the V100 it grows only 1.3 times,
   because the time per iteration per k-point falls as the batch fills the
   device.
2. **Tight tolerances fail.** On the V100, every test at the tightest SCF
   tolerance fails with eigensolver residuals near $1.5\times10^{-12}$
   against a requested $5\times10^{-14}$.
3. **Memory of dense band scans.** `band_minimum_on_segment` diagonalises 41
   k-points at once with the dense solver. The V100 failed on one allocation
   of 9.44 GiB.

Preparing the post and reviewing it changed all three:

- Problem 1 is mostly a bug, not a property of lockstep: LOBPCG converges
  the buffer bands, which the 2b rule says it should not.
- Problem 2 is the penalty on dropped directions, as the cluster diagnosis
  proposed, but through a mechanism that diagnosis did not see: near
  convergence the GPU drops directions at every iteration, the CPU almost
  never. Separately, the requested residual was below what the solver
  attains on either device, and on the CPU LOBPCG can climb back up by
  orders of magnitude once it is past that residual.
- Problem 3 is not specific to the GPU either (the same 9.45 GiB on the
  laptop), and it grows with the cutoff as well as with the number of
  k-points.

Out of scope: reduction of the k-grid by symmetry or time reversal, sharding
over several devices, other eigensolvers (Davidson, locking of converged
bands), LOBPCG on band paths, changes to the mixer, and implicit
differentiation through the SCF. Nothing here may change a converged result
beyond the tolerances that the 2a and 2b acceptance tests already use.

## Where the time goes

In the SCF each k-point is diagonalised by `lobpcg`, which is a
`lax.while_loop`. Under `vmap` a while loop runs until the condition is
false for every member of the batch. Members that have finished keep
computing, and their results are discarded. One SCF step therefore costs

$$
C_\text{step} \propto n_k \, n_\text{solve} \, \max_k I_k ,
$$

where $n_\text{solve}$ is the block width (needed bands plus buffer bands) and
$I_k$ is the number of iterations that k-point $\mathbf{k}$ needs. Without the
batch the cost would be the sum $\sum_k I_k$. The ratio
$\overline{I}/\max_k I_k$ is the *lockstep efficiency*.

The review measured it with a host callback inside the vmapped solver
(silicon, 12 Ha, SCF tolerance $10^{-9}$, one buffer band, summed over the
SCF):

| grid | $n_k$ | stopping test | $\sum\max_k I_k$ | $\sum\overline{I}$ | efficiency |
|:--:|:--:|:--|:--:|:--:|:--:|
| $2^3$ | 8 | all bands (today) | 193 | 153.6 | 0.80 |
| $2^3$ | 8 | needed bands | 175 | 148.5 | 0.85 |
| $3^3$ | 27 | all bands (today) | 370 | 236.3 | 0.64 |
| $3^3$ | 27 | needed bands | 203 | 158.9 | 0.78 |
| $4^3$ | 64 | all bands (today) | 344 | 219.3 | 0.64 |
| $4^3$ | 64 | needed bands | 226 | 168.1 | 0.74 |

The efficiency falls with $n_k$, then levels off. The stopping fix of the
next section raises it. After that fix, perfect per-k-point stopping would
save another 22–26 %. That is less than the stopping fix itself saves, so
lockstep proper is a second-order cost at these sizes. On the GPU, where a
fuller batch is cheaper per k-point, the gain from either will be smaller
than on the CPU.

## Stopping on the needed bands

The 2b post set the rule (decision 2 there): convergence is required only
for the bands the SCF needs, $N_\text{el}/2 + 1$, which include the first
conduction band. The eigensolver may carry buffer bands above them, which
are otherwise ignored. The SCF follows the rule in its final check (`eig_ok`
looks at the first `n_bands` columns). LOBPCG does not. It stops when every
one of its `n_solve` residuals is below the tolerance, buffer bands
included.

The standard convergence estimate for block LOBPCG [@knyazev2001] bounds the
error of Ritz pair $j$ through the separation of $\lambda_j$ from
$\lambda_{k+1}$, the first eigenvalue outside a block of width $k$. The
slowest band is therefore the one whose eigenvalue sits closest to
$\lambda_{k+1}$. That is usually the last band of the block, which is the
buffer band, and buffer bands exist to put distance between the needed
bands and $\lambda_{k+1}$. If the stopping test waits for the buffer band,
that distance buys nothing.

The review resolved this per k-point ($3^3$ grid, converged density, five
needed bands and one buffer band, cold start):

| $\lambda_7-\lambda_6$ (Ha) | k-points | slowest band | $I_k$, stop on 5 | $I_k$, stop on 6 |
|:--|:--:|:--:|:--:|:--:|
| $\approx 0$ | 9 | band 5 (needed) | 40–49 | 40–49 |
| 0.026 | 12 | band 6 (buffer) | 32–35 | 62–72 |
| 0.196 | 6 | band 6 (buffer) | 29–32 | 33–36 |

**An exact degeneracy at the block edge is harmless. A small non-zero gap is
what costs.** When $\lambda_6 = \lambda_7$, the block converges to some basis
of the degenerate eigenspace and the residual falls without obstruction.
When the gap is 0.026 Ha, the buffer band has to separate two nearly equal
eigenvalues and takes twice as long. Γ, where five bands cut through the
$\Gamma_{15}$ triplet, is the slowest k-point under either test. After the
fix it alone sets $\max_k I_k$ at this test size.

**Scratch check** (silicon, 12 Ha, SCF tolerance $10^{-9}$, one run each,
laptop; reproduced exactly by the review):

| grid | buffer bands | stopping test | $\sum \max_k I_k$ | wall time |
|:--:|:--:|:--:|:--:|:--:|
| $3^3$ | 1 | all bands (today) | 370 | 7.3 s |
| $3^3$ | 1 | needed bands | 203 | 4.1 s |
| $3^3$ | 3 | all bands | 330 | 9.5 s |
| $3^3$ | 3 | needed bands | 159 | 4.7 s |
| $4^3$ | 1 | all bands (today) | 344 | 16.5 s |
| $4^3$ | 1 | needed bands | 226 | 11.0 s |
| $4^3$ | 3 | all bands | 390 | 31.6 s |
| $4^3$ | 3 | needed bands | 160 | 14.7 s |

The total energy (to $3\times10^{-14}$ Ha) and the number of SCF steps are
the same in every row. On the CPU, stopping on the needed bands alone gives
1.5–2 times less wall time. Three buffer bands cut the iterations further,
but the wider block costs more per iteration than it saves; on $4^3$ the two
are close to even. On the GPU a wider block is cheaper per column, so the
balance there is open. 2b decided to settle it by measuring wall time on the
GPU, and this milestone does that measurement.

**Fix.** The eigensolver interface gains `n_converge`, the number of leading
bands that the stopping test covers (default: all, so existing callers are
unchanged). `lobpcg` honours it. The dense solver accepts and ignores it, as
it already ignores `tol`. The SCF passes `n_bands`. Buffer bands are then
what the 2b rule meant: directions that are carried, not converged, and
discarded.

The buffer columns feed nothing but the next warm start: occupations, the
gap guard and the returned orbitals all use the first `n_bands` columns. A
poor start column costs iterations; it cannot cost correctness, provided the
solver converges at all ([next section but one](#robust-stopping)).

## An adaptive eigensolver tolerance

The SCF asks the eigensolver for residuals of
$\tau = \max(\texttt{EIGEN\_TOL\_FRACTION}\cdot\varepsilon_\text{SCF},\ \text{floor})$
with `EIGEN_TOL_FRACTION` $= 0.05$, and requires
$\texttt{EIGEN\_CHECK\_FRACTION}\cdot\varepsilon_\text{SCF}$ $= 0.1\,\varepsilon_\text{SCF}$
at convergence (`eig_ok`). By default $\tau \approx 5\times10^{-11}$ Ha, also at
the first step, where the density error is of order one. An eigensolver
error far below the density error does not change the next density in any
way that survives mixing.

**Prior art.** Both reference codes the post was checked against tie the
diagonalisation tolerance to the SCF error (review, §2.7):

- DFTK (`AdaptiveDiagtol`, `src/scf/scf_callbacks.jl`) multiplies the norm
  of the density change by a ratio of 0.2, clamps the result to at most
  0.005, never lets it increase over the history, and treats the first two
  iterations separately. A comment there records size-dependent ratios
  that were tried, scaling with $1/N_\text{occ}$.
- Quantum ESPRESSO (`PW/src/electrons.f90`) sets the threshold to $10^{-2}$
  Ry at the second iteration, then to the minimum of its previous value and
  $0.1\,\delta/\max(1, N_\text{el})$, with $\delta$ the estimated SCF energy
  error in Ry, bounded below by $10^{-13}$. When the SCF error falls below
  what the threshold supports, it re-diagonalises in the same iteration
  with a lowered threshold.

Neither norm is ours: DFTK's density norm may differ from ours by the
volume element, and QE's threshold is on eigenvalues and relates two
energies. The ratios are not comparable as numbers.

**Rule.** At SCF step $i$, with $r_{i-1} = \lVert F(\rho_{i-1}) - \rho_{i-1}\rVert$
the residual of the previous step,

$$
\tau_i = \operatorname{clip}\!\left(\min\!\left(\tau_{i-1},\ \frac{c\, r_{i-1}}{N_\text{el}}\right),\ \tau_\text{min},\ \tau_\text{max}\right),
\qquad \tau_0 = \tau_\text{max},
$$

with $\tau_\text{min}$ the fixed tolerance of today (with the floor of the
[next section](#robust-stopping)) and $\tau_\text{max} = 5\times10^{-3}$ Ha,
the value both reference codes use. Three properties:

- **Non-increasing.** An Anderson step that overshoots raises $r$, but not
  $\tau$. Both reference codes do this.
- **Per electron.** $r$ is a norm over the whole cell and grows with the
  system; an eigensolver residual is per orbital. Without the $1/N_\text{el}$
  a default tuned on eight-electron silicon would be too loose by the system
  size on the aluminium supercells of the next milestone.
- **Units.** Our density norm is $(\Omega/N \sum r^2)^{1/2}$ in
  e·Bohr$^{-3/2}$ and residuals are in Ha, so $c$ is in Ha·Bohr$^{3/2}$. It
  is a setting, not a universal constant.

**Why a ratio rather than a derivation.** To first order, a residual $r$ of
an occupied orbital moves it out of the occupied subspace by about
$r/\Delta$, where $\Delta$ is the gap to the unoccupied states. Rotations
within the occupied subspace leave $\rho$ unchanged. The density error is
then of order $\sum_n f_n \lVert\psi_n\rVert_\infty\, r/\Delta$, with
constants that depend on the cell and the system. This justifies the form
$\tau \propto r$, with a constant that shrinks with the gap. It does not
give a value of $c$ that is both safe and useful. The default is set by
measurement, and the acceptance tests check that the converged result does
not depend on it.

**Convergence is declared on a tight evaluation.** `fixed_point` stops when
$\lVert F(\rho_i) - \rho_i\rVert < \varepsilon_\text{SCF}$. If that $F$ was
evaluated with a loose $\tau_i$, the residual itself is uncertain. The
design, which is the one QE uses:

- **Refine inside $F$.** If the density residual of a loose evaluation is
  below $\varepsilon_\text{SCF}$, $F$ re-diagonalises at $\tau_\text{min}$,
  warm-started from the loose orbitals, and returns the refined density.
  The predicate is a scalar outside the k-point `vmap`, so the `lax.cond`
  is a real branch; under `vmap` with a batched predicate it would evaluate
  both branches. `fixed_point` stays generic, and at a converged point $F$
  is always the tight map, which implicit differentiation will need.
- **Latch.** Once a step has refined, $\tau = \tau_\text{min}$ for every later
  step. Without the latch, a loose evaluation can dip below
  $\varepsilon_\text{SCF}$, refine to a residual above it, and repeat this
  at the next step.

This also removes a collision the review found: with $c\,r_{i-1}$ near
$0.1\,\varepsilon_\text{SCF}$, the converging step would sit exactly at the
`eig_ok` threshold. With refinement the final accuracy is always
$\tau_\text{min}$, whatever $c$ is.

**Scratch check** (silicon $3^3$, 12 Ha, stopping on the needed bands,
refinement without latch, $\tau_\text{max} = 10^{-2}$ Ha, no $1/N_\text{el}$, the
bounded penalty below; not reproduced by the review, which had no
implementation of the rule):

| $\varepsilon_\text{SCF}$ | $c$ | SCF steps | $\sum \max_k I_k$ | wall time |
|:--:|:--:|:--:|:--:|:--:|
| $10^{-9}$ | fixed $\tau$ | 8 | 203 | 4.1 s |
| $10^{-9}$ | 0.1 | 11 | 124 | 2.7 s |
| $10^{-9}$ | 0.01 | 11 | 113 | 2.6 s |
| $10^{-12}$ | 0.1 | 15 | 89 | 2.1 s |
| $10^{-12}$ | 0.01 | 15 | 229 | 5.8 s |

Energies agree to $10^{-12}$ Ha with the fixed-tolerance runs.

- The inexact $F$ costs SCF steps (8 → 11). Each step also costs a
  potential, a density and an energy, so wall time gains less than the
  iterations. On larger grids, where the eigensolver dominates more, the
  balance should improve; this is to be measured.
- A refinement costs about 3–4 LOBPCG iterations per decade of residual
  (review, §2.8, measured directly). Losing the search directions $P$ at the
  restart costs about one. The 64 iterations of the refinement at
  $10^{-9}$, $c = 0.1$ are therefore not explained by the restart. The likely
  explanation is that it fired at more than one step, which the latch
  prevents and the refinement counter will show.
- The $c = 0.01$, $10^{-12}$ row is not explained either, and before the
  penalty change the same run hit the 300-iteration cap three times. Both
  are consistent with the blow-up of [the next section](#robust-stopping),
  which this milestone fixes. The implementation must explain this row.

**Defaults.** $\tau_\text{max} = 5\times10^{-3}$ Ha; $c$ is set during
implementation by measurement on the $3^3$ and $4^3$ grids, starting from the
silicon equivalent of the scratch check's 0.1 ($c = 0.8$ with the
$1/N_\text{el}$). Both are `SCFOptions`, and $c = 0$ recovers the fixed
tolerance.

**What does not change.** `energy` and its gradients use the converged,
stop-gradiented orbitals, and the rule above ensures those came from a tight
evaluation. Forces, weight derivatives and the Hellmann–Feynman argument of
2a are unaffected. `energy` runs without a history, so the new diagnostics
are not available in force runs. Diagnosing the adaptive tolerance there
means running `scf` at the same settings.

## Robust stopping

### Near the attainable residual, LOBPCG can climb back

Forced to 200 iterations with an unreachable tolerance, the review tracked
the largest residual of one k-point: $1.6\times10^{-5}$, $1.3\times10^{-10}$,
$6.2\times10^{-13}$ at iteration 60, then back up to $6\times10^{-8}$, after
which it moved over five orders of magnitude. The eigenvalues stayed
accurate to $3\times10^{-14}$ throughout, as expected from the $r^2/\Delta$
law. The damage is in the vectors, about $r/\Delta \approx 2\times10^{-6}$, and
the density is built from the vectors.

The per-iteration record ([below](#evidence-per-iteration-on-both-devices))
confirms it on the CPU. Forced past its best residual, silicon climbs to
$2$–$9\times10^{-8}$ in 11 of the 12 forced runs on the laptop and the cluster
CPU, with either penalty, and mostly without dropping any direction after
the first iteration, so the penalty plays no part. It then falls back, to
$4\times10^{-14}$–$2.4\times10^{-13}$ at iteration 300. H₂ does not climb, and
neither does silicon on the V100 with the bounded penalty.

At the real tolerance the climb matters only when a run's best falls short
of the tolerance, so that it keeps iterating. That happened once in the 24
CPU runs: silicon from one start on the laptop reached $4.6\times10^{-13}$ at
iteration 51, climbed to $7\times10^{-9}$, and needed 186 iterations instead of
49–51. It reproduces exactly on the laptop, but not on the cluster CPU,
which follows a different trajectory from the same start. The climb is
common once a run is past its attainable residual, and rarely reached in
practice as long as the requested tolerance is attainable. It is not the
cause of the GPU failures, which plateau instead (next section).

`lobpcg` returns its last iterate, not its best, so a run that reaches
`max_iter` during such a climb returns something far worse than what it
had. The SCF then fails loudly, through `eig_ok`, but with a residual that
says nothing about what the solver could reach.

**Fix** (both standard; @duersch2018 discuss them together with the basis
problems of the next section):

- **A stagnation stop.** Leave the loop when $\max_j r_j$, over the bands of
  the stopping test, has not improved by a factor 0.8 over the last 5
  iterations. The running best is one scalar in the loop state.
- **Return the best iterate.** Carry the block with the smallest
  $\max_j r_j$ seen. That is one extra $(n_\text{pad}, n_\text{solve})$ block,
  negligible against the FFT workspace.

A stagnation stop before the requested tolerance is not a success. The
caller sees the residuals it got, as now, and the SCF's `eig_ok` decides.

### The floor scales with the operator

`EIGEN_FLOOR` $= 2\times10^{-14}$ was meant as "$\lVert H\rVert\epsilon$". At
the test size $\lVert H\rVert_2\,\epsilon_\text{mach}$ is $2.6\times10^{-15}$
(physical plane waves) to $5.3\times10^{-15}$ (with the padding sentinel). The
smallest max-over-bands residual LOBPCG reaches is $2$–$5\times10^{-14}$, about
ten times more, from rounding accumulated over the Rayleigh–Ritz, QR and
inverse steps. The V100, with the penalty changed, reached
$2.9\times10^{-14}$ (Si) and $3.7\times10^{-14}$ (H₂). So:

- `tol` $= 10^{-12}$ asks for $5\times10^{-14}$, met with a margin of 1–2.5 on
  either device;
- any `tol` below $4\times10^{-13}$ asks for $2\times10^{-14}$, which is not
  attainable, and produces the drift above;
- $\lVert H\rVert$ grows with the cutoff, so an absolute floor that is
  attainable at 12 Ha is not at 40 Ha.

**Fix.** The floor becomes a property of each k-point's operator:

$$
\tau_\text{floor}(\mathbf{k}) = \kappa\,\epsilon_\text{mach}\,\lVert H_\mathbf{k}\rVert_\text{est},
$$

with $\lVert H_\mathbf{k}\rVert_\text{est}$ an inexpensive upper estimate from
the operator (the largest diagonal element of the prepared terms, which the
kinetic energy dominates at any useful cutoff), and $\kappa$ measured: the
attainable multiple (about 10) with a margin, so that the floor is reached
with room to spare on both devices. $\tau_\text{min}$ and the `eig_ok` check
use this floor in place of the constant. At the test size it will lie near
$10^{-13}$, so the tight-tolerance tests ask the eigensolver for about
$10^{-13}$ rather than $5\times10^{-14}$. The density error that follows is far
below anything those tests resolve. The SCF tolerances themselves remain
absolute.

The review also suggested a relative stopping test,
$r_j \le \texttt{tol}\,(\lVert H\rVert + |\theta_j|)$ [@duersch2018]. It would
make every eigensolver tolerance in the code dimensionless, a wider change
than this milestone needs, and was not adopted.

## The Rayleigh–Ritz penalty

Each LOBPCG iteration orthonormalises the residual directions $W$ and the
previous directions $P$ against the block $X$ and drops near-dependent
directions. Shapes are fixed, so a dropped direction becomes a zero column
of $Q$. The Rayleigh–Ritz matrix on $S = [X, Q]$ is

$$
T = S^\dagger H S + \operatorname{diag}(\sigma\,\mathbb{1}_\text{dropped}),
$$

and today $\sigma = 10^3(\max|T| + 1)$. The lowest $k$ eigenpairs of $T$ give
the new block. A dropped column of $Q$ is exactly zero, so its row and
column of $S^\dagger H S$ are zero. $T$ is then block diagonal, and the
dropped part is $\sigma$ times the identity. Choosing $\sigma$ is the same as
removing the dropped directions, provided $\sigma$ lies above the $k$ lowest
eigenvalues of the kept part. In fixed shapes, the penalty already *is* the
removal. Its value is the only question.

**A bound from interlacing.** $X$ holds the current Ritz vectors, with Ritz
values $\varepsilon_1 \le \dots \le \varepsilon_k$, and
$X^\dagger H X = \operatorname{diag}(\varepsilon)$ is a principal submatrix of
the kept part of $T$. By the Cauchy interlacing theorem [@parlett1998], the
$j$-th smallest eigenvalue of the kept part is at most $\varepsilon_j$. So
any $\sigma > \varepsilon_k$ keeps dropped directions out. The choice is

$$
\sigma = \varepsilon_k + (\varepsilon_k - \varepsilon_1) + 1\ \text{Ha}.
$$

The 1 Ha is dimensionful, which the atomic-units convention makes
unambiguous; it keeps a margin when the Ritz values coincide, and at $k = 1$
gives $\sigma = \varepsilon_1 + 1$ Ha. Two sources of rounding are covered by
the margin by many orders of magnitude:

- The Ritz values are current, not stale: the loop recomputes them from
  $X^\dagger A X$ after the QR step at the end of each iteration. Their
  rounding is about $10^{-14}$ Ha.
- The code solves a standard eigenproblem for $T$, which assumes
  $S^\dagger S = I$. The non-orthonormality of $[X, Q]$ enters as about
  $\lVert H\rVert\,\delta_\text{orth} \approx 10^{-12}$ Ha.

**Why its size matters.** A backward-stable `eigh` has absolute errors of
order $\epsilon_\text{mach}\lVert T\rVert$. With today's $\sigma$, $\lVert T\rVert$
is thousands of Ha whenever a direction is dropped, against 3–10 Ha with
the bound. The error of the Ritz pairs we keep grows by the same factor.
Whether that matters depends on how often directions are dropped, which the
three explanations disagreed about.

### Evidence: per iteration, on both devices

The earlier GPU diagnosis compared end states, one run per variant: the
GPU plateaued near $10^{-12}$, and both moving the Rayleigh–Ritz `eigh` to the
CPU and lowering $\sigma$ removed the plateau. Three explanations fit that:

1. *(cluster diagnosis)* the penalty inflates $\lVert T\rVert$, and the GPU's
   `eigh` is not accurate enough relative to it;
2. *(draft of this post)* the same happens on the CPU at tolerances near
   $10^{-13}$, where the bounded $\sigma$ removed a stall in an SCF scratch
   check;
3. *(review)* directions are dropped only at the first iteration, so the
   penalty is inactive afterwards, and the failures are the climb of the
   previous section; one run per variant cannot tell a penalty effect from
   a different trajectory.

They make different predictions for one number: whether directions are
dropped after the first iteration on the GPU. An instrumented copy of
`lobpcg` (`shephex/scripts/aicloud/lobpcg_trajectory.py`) records, per
iteration, the residual, the directions dropped in each orthonormalisation
pass, $\max|T|$ including the penalty, and the backward error of the
Rayleigh–Ritz `eigh`, $\max_j\lVert T c_j - \theta_j c_j\rVert$ over the pairs
kept. It ran on the V100 and the CPU of the same node, and on the laptop,
from three random starts per variant, on the two problems of the earlier
diagnosis, at the SCF's tight eigensolver tolerance $5\times10^{-14}$
(`reference/gpu_lobpcg_floor/lobpcg_trajectory.json`). Ranges over the three
starts, cluster node, stopping at the tolerance:

| problem | device | penalty | iterations | final residual | drops after iteration 1 |
|:--|:--|:--|:--:|:--:|:--:|
| H₂ | CPU | today | 71–77 | 4.0–4.8e-14 | 0–1 |
| H₂ | CPU | bound | 70–77 | 3.0–4.8e-14 | 0 |
| H₂ | V100 | today | 300 (cap) | 0.8–1.3e-12 | 744–755 |
| H₂ | V100 | bound | 69–75 | 3.1–4.2e-14 | 46–58 |
| H₂ | V100 | today, `eigh` on host | 70–76 | 3.6–4.0e-14 | 0 |
| Si | CPU | today | 49–51 | 2.5–3.5e-14 | 0 |
| Si | CPU | bound | 49–50 | 2.6–3.1e-14 | 0 |
| Si | V100 | today | 300 (cap) | 3.4–6.2e-12 | 1572–1588 |
| Si | V100 | bound | 50–51 | 2.8–4.8e-14 | 48–60 |
| Si | V100 | today, `eigh` on host | 49 | 2.5–4.1e-14 | 0 |

The trajectories show the mechanism directly. On the V100, with either
penalty, the first late drop comes at the same iteration (32–34), once the
residual is between $10^{-8}$ and $10^{-5}$. From then on 1–6 directions are
dropped at every iteration. With today's $\sigma$, those iterations have
$\max|T|$ between 1300 and 7600 Ha and a Rayleigh–Ritz backward error up to
$2$–$7\times10^{-12}$, against about $10^{-15}$ before. The residual stops at
that level, $10^{-12}$ for H₂ and $4\times10^{-12}$ for Si, for the remaining 250
iterations: a plateau, not a climb. With the bound, the same drops happen,
$\max|T|$ stays below 6 Ha, the backward error at those iterations stays
below $7\times10^{-15}$, and the runs converge in as many iterations as on the
CPU. With the `eigh` on the host there are no late drops at all.

So, for each explanation:

1. **Holds on the GPU**, with the mechanism made explicit: the GPU drops
   directions at every iteration near convergence, each drop activates the
   penalty, and the residual cannot fall below the Rayleigh–Ritz error the
   penalty causes.
2. **Wrong.** On the CPU, late drops are rare (0–1 per run at the real
   tolerance), and the penalty does not change the iteration count. The
   scratch-check stall was the climb of the previous section, and the
   bounded $\sigma$ only changed which trajectory the run followed.
3. **Right about the CPU, not the GPU.** The review's observation that
   directions are dropped only at the first iteration holds on the CPU and
   is the reason the penalty is harmless there. The climb is real and
   common on the CPU once a run is past its attainable residual, but it is
   a separate phenomenon from the GPU plateau.

**Not established:** why the GPU's Rayleigh–Ritz `eigh` leads to late drops
when the host's does not. With the bound the GPU's backward error is about
$10^{-15}$, as on the host, yet the drops still happen. The fix does not
depend on the answer, since the drops then cost nothing. Near-dependence of
$W$ and $P$ near convergence is a known weakness of LOBPCG's basis
[@duersch2018].

**Limits.** One GPU model, one job, two small problems, three starts each;
the laptop and the cluster CPU differ in which rare trajectories they
follow.

**Decision.** The bounded $\sigma$ is adopted as the fix for the GPU
failures, on this evidence and because it is derived. The stagnation stop
and best-iterate return of the previous section are kept as protection
against the climb, which they also cover on the GPU should it occur there.

## Memory of batched k-points

The dense solver builds $H$ by applying it to the identity, so one k-point
holds $n_\text{pad}$ wavefunctions on the FFT grid in several intermediates.
Under `vmap` all k-points do so at once. XLA's own estimate of the peak
temporaries of the compiled program (`memory_analysis()`, so measurable
without a GPU), for the failing test (LDA silicon at 12 Ha,
$n_\text{pad} = 548$, FFT grid $24^3$): 0.23 GiB for one k-point, 9.45 GiB for
the segment's 41.

The per-k-point figure grows with the cutoff, as $n_\text{grid}\,n_\text{pad}$
(review, one k-point of silicon, dense solver):

| $E_\text{cut}$ (Ha) | $n_\text{pad}$ | FFT grid | temporaries |
|:--:|:--:|:--:|:--:|
| 12 | 528 | $24^3$ | 0.22 GiB |
| 20 | 1174 | $30^3$ | 0.97 GiB |
| 30 | 2085 | $36^3$ | 2.97 GiB |
| 40 | 3263 | $45^3$ | 9.04 GiB |

Chunking over k-points alone therefore fixes the band scan only at the test
cutoff. At 40 Ha, which the 2b convergence table reaches, one k-point is as
large as the whole failing allocation.

**Fix, at two levels**, both with `jax.lax.map(..., batch_size=...)` (JAX
0.12), which applies a function to chunks of a batch: within a chunk it is
`vmap`, and chunks run one after another.

- **Columns in the dense solver.** `dense_eigensolver` applies the operator
  to the identity in column chunks. Its temporaries are then bounded by the
  chunk, independently of $n_\text{pad}$ and of $n_k$. Only the
  $n_\text{pad}\times n_\text{pad}$ matrix itself remains.
- **k-points.** `band_structure` and the SCF gain an optional
  `k_batch_size` (default `None`: one batch, as today). k-points remain a
  batch dimension in the sense of CLAUDE.md: the per-k function is unchanged
  and still vmapped, and sharding can later split the k-axis across devices
  with chunking inside each.

Results must not depend on either chunk size beyond rounding. Two details
for the implementation: `lax.map` with a chunk size that does not divide the
batch compiles a second program for the remainder, which inside the SCF's
while loop is a second copy of the whole per-k pipeline, so chunk sizes
should divide the batch or the batch be padded and masked; and `lax.map`
maps one pytree, so the two-argument per-k functions need a wrapper.

**The SCF.** Its peak memory grows linearly with $n_k$: on the V100 by
7.4 MB per k-point, 3.8 GB at $8^3$, which extrapolates to about 13 GB at
$12^3$ on the same cell. Lockstep is a second-order cost after the stopping
fix (see [above](#where-the-time-goes)), so the SCF's chunk size is chosen
for memory and device occupancy, not for lockstep, and stays at one batch by
default until measured.

**Band scans stay dense.** LOBPCG applies $H$ to $2k$ columns per iteration;
at 40–50 cold-start iterations and $k = 6$ that is 480–600 applications per
k-point, no fewer than the dense solver's 548 at 12 Ha. The dense solver
also returns every eigenvalue and cannot mis-converge. `band_structure`
passes the solver no start, preconditioner or tolerance, and has no residual
check, so LOBPCG on band paths is its own design, for a milestone where the
cutoff makes it pay.

## Observability

The SCF history (2026-11-10, "SCF observability") gains per step:

- `eig_tol`, the tolerance $\tau_i$ used;
- `eig_iters_mean`, the mean of $I_k$ over k-points, next to the existing
  maximum `eig_iters`, so the lockstep efficiency is visible in the log and
  on the performance page;
- `refined`, whether the step re-diagonalised at $\tau_\text{min}$
  (`eig_iters` counts both diagonalisations of such a step);
- `eig_drops`, the largest number of directions dropped by LOBPCG after its
  first iteration, over k-points and iterations, and `eig_stagnated`,
  whether any k-point left by the stagnation stop.

`lobpcg` returns the corresponding diagnostics when asked, as it already
returns its iteration count.

## Invariants and acceptance criteria

The physics invariants of CLAUDE.md are unaffected, and the existing 2a and
2b acceptance tests must pass unchanged, including the tight-tolerance tests
at $\varepsilon_\text{SCF} = 10^{-12}$ on the CPU. New tests, to be written as
failing tests before implementation:

1. **Stopping test.** `lobpcg` with `n_converge = m` returns the first $m$
   residuals below `tol`; the first $m$ eigenvalues agree with the dense
   solver within the bound that `tol` implies. With `n_converge` equal to the
   block width it behaves as today.
2. **Independence of settings.** The converged SCF energy, density and
   eigenvalues of silicon on the 2³ test grid do not depend on
   `buffer_bands` ∈ {0, 1, 3}, on $c$ (including $c = 0$), or on
   `k_batch_size`, within the tolerances 2b already uses for comparing
   converged states.
3. **Tight convergence.** With the adaptive tolerance, every converged SCF
   has `eig_ok`; the history shows the last step at $\tau_\text{min}$, $\tau$
   non-increasing, and no refinement after the first.
4. **Penalty.** Dropped directions are never selected (a property test on
   blocks with forced dependence, including the first iteration, where
   $P = 0$), and $\sigma$ is the bound above.
5. **Robust stopping.** Asked for a tolerance below its floor, `lobpcg`
   leaves by the stagnation stop well before `max_iter`, and returns a block
   whose residual is the best it reached. At the test sizes of silicon and
   H₂, `lobpcg` reaches $\tau_\text{floor}$ on the CPU.
6. **The unexplained scratch row.** Silicon $3^3$ at
   $\varepsilon_\text{SCF} = 10^{-12}$ with the smallest tested $c$ converges
   within an iteration budget set from the $c = 0$ run, not just below the
   cap.
7. **Cost.** On the $3^3$ grid, which the force tests already use, the summed
   $\max_k I_k$ and $\overline{I}$ over the SCF at the default settings are at
   most stated budgets, measured on the current commit when the tests are
   written. The $2^3$ grid cannot see the stopping fix (193 → 175).
8. **Memory.** The compiled temporaries of the dense solver for one k-point
   are bounded independently of $n_\text{pad}$ (checked at 12 and 20 Ha), the
   band sampling of `band_minimum_on_segment` for the case that failed on the
   V100 stays below 2 GiB, and chunked and unchunked results agree to
   rounding.

**On the clusters** (records in `reference/`, not pass/fail tests, since
they cannot run at render time):

- the full test suite on the V100 passes, against 634 of 642 today;
- the per-iteration diagnosis is repeated against the implemented `lobpcg`
  on the V100, which must converge from every start with late drops
  present and a Rayleigh–Ritz backward error near $10^{-15}$;
- the k-grid scan is repeated on biocloud and aicloud; the performance page
  shows time per k-point and SCF step, $\sum\max_k I_k$, the lockstep
  efficiency and peak memory against the 2b runs;
- on the V100, the scan is repeated for `buffer_bands` ∈ {0, 1, 2, 3} and a
  few chunk sizes, to settle the defaults 2b left open.

## Decisions from review

1. **Stopping on the needed bands: adopted as drafted.** The reasoning is
   narrowed to "the band closest to $\lambda_{k+1}$ is slowest", and the
   degeneracy paragraph now says that an exact degeneracy at the edge is
   harmless and a small gap is what costs.
2. **The bounded penalty: adopted.** The review accepted the bound but
   questioned whether it is the cause of the GPU failures. A per-iteration
   record from three starts per variant, run after the review, showed that
   it is ([evidence](#evidence-per-iteration-on-both-devices)). The solver
   reports late drops so that this stays visible.
3. **Stagnation stop and best-iterate return: added to the milestone.** The
   review found LOBPCG climbing back from near its attainable residual. The
   per-iteration record shows it in most forced silicon runs on the CPU,
   with either penalty, but only once at the real tolerance, and not as the
   cause of the GPU failures. It is a failure the solver should survive,
   and the attainable floor of decision 4 keeps runs from reaching it.
4. **`EIGEN_FLOOR` scales with $\lVert H_\mathbf{k}\rVert$**, with a measured
   multiple of $\epsilon_\text{mach}$. Of the three options (a larger constant,
   an operator-scaled floor, a relative stopping test), the scaled floor was
   chosen with the project lead: it holds at any cutoff and leaves the SCF
   tolerances absolute.
5. **The adaptive tolerance** is non-increasing, divided by $N_\text{el}$,
   capped at $5\times10^{-3}$ Ha, refined inside $F$ (as QE does) with a latch,
   and its refinements are counted. The default $c$ is measured during
   implementation.
6. **Memory: column chunking in the dense solver as well as k-chunking.** The
   memory criterion is stated per k-point and independent of $n_\text{pad}$.
7. **Band scans stay on the dense solver** (open question 4).
8. **The SCF's k-chunk size is chosen for memory, not lockstep, and defaults
   to one batch** (open question 5), since lockstep proper is second-order
   after the stopping fix.
9. **The cost budget is set on the $3^3$ grid** and asserts on the mean
   iterations as well as the maximum.
10. **Scope: no physics in disguise** (open question 6). All configurations
    the review ran agree on the energy to $3\times10^{-14}$ Ha.
11. **Not verified.** The adaptive-tolerance table was not reproduced by the
    review, and the reference-code descriptions are the review's reading of
    DFTK and QE sources, not checked again here. The direction of the GPU
    gain is a prediction from the scan, to be measured. Why the GPU drops
    directions near convergence and the CPU does not is open.
